rules.statement: Do not keep state that must outlive a single request in process memory (static fields, singleton dictionaries, in-memory caches used as the source of truth); put durable state in the database and shared ephemeral state in a shared distributed store abstraction such as IDistributedCache.
rules.why: Services must be correct with several interchangeable replicas; any replica must be able to serve any request, and a replaced replica must not lose state that matters.
rules.check: Look for new static or singleton-held mutable collections, ConcurrentDictionary stores, or IMemoryCache entries that hold sessions, single-use tokens, nonces, or other cross-request state instead of using the database or a distributed store.

rules.statement: Do not design features that depend on sticky sessions or on a request being routed back to the same replica.
rules.why: Any replica serves any request; sticky routing breaks redundancy and replica replacement.
rules.check: Flag code that assumes a follow-up request hits the same process (e.g. state stashed locally between authorize and callback steps, session affinity configuration).

rules.statement: Do not write durable data to the local filesystem; persist it to the database or an object store.
rules.why: Nodes and pods are disposable and containers run with read-only root filesystems, so local-disk data is lost on replacement.
rules.check: Look for File/Directory write APIs, local file-based key rings, or local SQLite/file stores used for data that must persist.

rules.statement: Read configuration from the environment via the configuration system rather than from hard-coded values or files edited in place, and never commit secrets to source control.
rules.why: Twelve-factor configuration and secure-by-default principles: secrets live in the secret store or KMS, never in Git.
rules.check: Flag connection strings, keys, passwords or tokens committed in appsettings, code, or test fixtures meant for real environments, and hard-coded environment-specific values.

rules.statement: Write logs to stdout through the standard logging pipeline rather than to log files managed by the application.
rules.why: Twelve-factor: logs go to stdout and are collected by the platform; local files violate read-only filesystems and statelessness.
rules.check: Look for file log sinks or custom file-writing loggers added to the host.

rules.statement: Emit metrics, logs and traces through OpenTelemetry rather than vendor-specific telemetry SDKs.
rules.why: Observability must use open standards so vendors can be swapped by replacing a component.
rules.check: Flag new dependencies on vendor-specific telemetry/APM SDKs or custom metric exporters bypassing OpenTelemetry.

rules.statement: Give every outbound call to another service a timeout and, where retried, bounded retries with jitter, and degrade gracefully on failure.
rules.why: Design for failure: an unbounded or hanging dependency call takes the service down with it.
rules.check: Look for HttpClient or other remote calls without a configured timeout, unbounded retry loops, or fixed-delay retries without jitter.

rules.statement: Make database schema changes expand/contract so the previous and new application versions can run side by side against the same schema.
rules.why: Rollouts are progressive and rolling, so old and new versions run concurrently.
rules.check: Flag migrations that rename or drop columns/tables, or add non-nullable columns without defaults, in the same release that changes the code using them.

rules.statement: Honor the host's shutdown cancellation token so in-flight work drains and the process stops gracefully, and do not rely on in-process background queues for work that must survive replica replacement.
rules.why: Processes must start fast and shut down gracefully; in-process job dispatch loses in-flight jobs when a replica is replaced.
rules.check: Look for background services ignoring stoppingToken, fire-and-forget tasks, or in-memory job queues used for work that must not be lost.
